'''Evolutionary data mining''', or '''genetic data mining''' is an [[umbrella term]] for any [[data mining]] using [[evolutionary algorithm]]s. While it can be used for mining data from [[DNA sequence]]s,<ref name=wai-ho>Wai-Ho Au, Keith C. C. Chan, and Xin Yao. [https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/stamp/stamp.jsp?arnumber=1255389&isnumber=28075 "A Novel Evolutionary Data Mining Algorithm With Applications to Churn Prediction"], ''[[IEEE]]'', retrieved on 2008-12-4.</ref> it is not limited to biological contexts and can be used in any classification-based prediction scenario, which helps "predict the value ... of a user-specified goal attribute based on the values of other attributes."<ref name=freitas>Freitas, Alex A. [http://neuro.bstu.by/our/Data-mining/fereitas-ga.pdf "A Survey of Evolutionary Algorithms for Data Mining and Knowledge Discovery"], ''[[Pontifícia Universidade Católica do Paraná]]'', Retrieved on 2008-12-4.</ref> For instance, a banking institution might want to predict whether a customer's [[Credit (finance)|credit]] would be "good" or "bad" based on their age, income and current savings.<ref name=freitas/> Evolutionary algorithms for data mining work by creating a series of [[random]] rules to be checked against a training [[dataset]].<ref name= jiawei /> The rules which most closely fit the data are selected and are [[mutated]].<ref name= jiawei /> The process is [[iteration|iterated]] many times and eventually, a rule will arise that approaches 100% similarity with the training data.<ref name= freitas /> This rule is then checked against a test dataset, which was previously invisible to the genetic algorithm.<ref name= freitas />

==Process==

===Data preparation===

Before [[database]]s can be mined for data using evolutionary algorithms, it first has to be cleaned,<ref name= freitas /> which means incomplete, noisy or inconsistent data should be repaired. It is imperative that this be done before the mining takes place, as it will help the algorithms produce more accurate results.<ref name=jiawei>Jiawei Han, Micheline Kamber ''Data Mining: Concepts and Techniques'' (2006), [[Morgan Kaufmann]], {{ISBN|1-55860-901-6}}</ref>

If data comes from more than one database, they can be integrated, or combined, at this point.<ref name=jiawei /> When dealing with large datasets, it might be beneficial to also reduce the amount of data being handled.<ref name=jiawei/> One common method of data reduction works by getting a [[Normalization (statistics)|normalized]] sample of data from the database, resulting in much faster, yet statistically equivalent results.<ref name=jiawei/>

At this point, the data is split into two equal but mutually exclusive elements, a test and a training dataset.<ref name= freitas /> The training dataset will be used to let rules evolve which match it closely.<ref name= freitas /> The test dataset will then either confirm or deny these rules.<ref name= freitas />

===Data mining===

Evolutionary algorithms work by trying to emulate natural [[evolution]].<ref name=jiawei /> First, a random series of "rules" are set on the training dataset, which try to generalize the data into formulas.<ref name=jiawei /> The rules are checked, and the ones that fit the data best are kept, the rules that do not fit the data are discarded.<ref name=jiawei /> The rules that were kept are then mutated, and multiplied to create new rules.<ref name=jiawei />

This process iterates as necessary in order to produce a rule that matches the dataset as closely as possible.<ref name=jiawei /> When this rule is obtained, it is then checked against the test dataset.<ref name= freitas /> If the rule still matches the data, then the rule is valid and is kept.<ref name= freitas /> If it does not match the data, then it is discarded and the process begins by selecting random rules again.<ref name= freitas />
